extracted.intended_audience: poets, students of poetry, and literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for poets and critics on crafting and judging poetic diction — how to balance natural speech, metre/rhyme, imagination, and taste so verse is neither merely prosaic nor artificially ornate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid prosaic diction (prosaism)
rubrics_metrics.description: The style is justly blamable as prosaic when the words and the order of the words would find their appropriate place in prose, but are not suitable to metrical composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Hazlitt cites passages from Daniel’s CIVIL WARS and other writers to show lines whose diction corresponds to prose and are therefore called 'prosaic Daniel.' He notes that entire sequences may be transcribable as prose, and that this incorrespondency of diction to metre is a defect even when sense and feeling are present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve metrical audibility (meter must not be merely visual)
rubrics_metrics.description: Metre should not be metre to the eye only; a poem must keep its metric identity so that it cannot be rendered unrecognizable as verse by simple transcription into prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If successive lines can be rendered as prose without loss, or if in blank verse restoring one or two words suffices to make them prose, the metre has become only a visual feature. For rhyme, merely exchanging final words for synonyms might make lines read like prose. This detracts from poetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substance: sense, feeling, and interesting subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Lines are not bad merely because they are 'unpoetic'; they are bad when they are empty of sense and feeling. Good sense, weighty meaning, and feeling are prerequisites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt contrasts a trivial nursery rhyme ('I put my hat upon my head...') to show that absence of sense/feeling — not simple prosaic diction — is what renders lines worthless. A poem should have a subject treated with feeling and dignified language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal facility: apt expression that fits rhyme and metre
rubrics_metrics.description: A key poetical talent is the ability to seek the apt expression of a thought and simultaneously to find the rhyme and the metre with it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Garve’s praise of Gellert exemplifies this: verses that read like natural speech yet are 'perfectly correct as to the measure of the syllables and the rhyme.' Hazlitt cites Spenser, Waller, and Cotton as examples of achieving this balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination/meditation over mere imitation of colloquial speech
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet must rely on imagination (meditation and inward experience) rather than slavishly copying the language of market or uncultivated society to obtain suitable diction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt asks how a poet would distinguish language for suppressed versus indulged anger, or rage versus jealousy: by imagination and insight into human nature, not by hunting for examples in low society. The poet’s inward experience provides the right discriminations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Govern style by grammar, logic, psychology and Taste
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet’s style should be regulated by the principles of grammar, logic, and psychology and by a cultivated taste — knowledge of material and spiritual facts applied with good sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt argues that ignoring these principles makes one 'no poet, but a silly or presumptuous usurper.' Taste emerges from disciplined knowledge rendered instinctive by habit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rhetorical caprices and forced juxtapositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject figures and constructions that excite surprise by compulsory juxtaposition of incompatible things — a species of contrived wit rather than true imaginative expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of the offending mode include extravagant images like 'the hills reflect the image of thy voice' or the mad exuberances of some Pindaric imitations. Such devices are works of will and artifice, not of genuine poetic insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish genuine poetic fervour from pseudo-poesy and hysteric excess
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclude 'madness prepense' and hysteric over-exertions — passionate odes aimed at abstract terms that merely startle without authentic feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt points to numerous odes in magazines and collections (e.g., Odes to 'jealousy', 'Hope', 'Oblivion') as examples of poetical excess that resemble affected rant rather than true fervour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neutral/common style (lingua communis) can be excellent
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a neutral style common to prose and poetry — ordinary, conversational diction — which, when handled skillfully, can be dignified, attractive, and metrically correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt cites Gellert, Spenser, Chaucer, Herbert, and others as masters of this 'well-languaged' style where everything is expressed as one would speak yet remains fully poetic and metrically satisfying (examples from Chaucer's Troilus and Creseide and Herbert's poems).

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain an individual, recognizable poetic voice
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet’s diction may be distinctive and consistent across works; a characteristic diction that is recognisable is a mark of excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt notes that Wordsworth’s style is so characteristic that short quotations are immediately recognized as his. Consistent individuality of diction is a virtue when it arises from genuine sensibility and thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry cannot be produced by external, mechanical rules alone
rubrics_metrics.description: If poetry could be produced by a set of external rules alone, it would cease to be poetry — the rules of imagination are intrinsic powers of production, not prescriptive formulas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt emphasizes that rule-giving from without would reduce poetry to mere machinery ('morphosis, not poiaesis') and that the principles of the Imagination are formative powers rather than checklists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suit diction to the specific emotion or state
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet must discriminate between the language appropriate to different emotional states (suppressed vs indulged anger; rage vs jealousy) and render those differences authentically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such distinctions are arrived at by creative power and inward perception, not by copying observed speech; the poet intuitively knows what intermixture of volition the composing state justifies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer cultivated, elegant colloquialism over slavish market-speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopting the raw speech of market, wake, or plough-field is not the necessary path to naturalness; often the cultivated, unaffected speech of well-bred people supplies the pure English best suited to refined poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt points to 'elegant and unaffected women' as mistresses of 'pure English and undefiled' and cites Chaucer/Henry-era pronunciation and gentlemanly expression (Herbert) as models of natural yet dignified diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend to historical/pronunciation resources when using older language
rubrics_metrics.description: Older orthography and historical pronunciation (e.g., Chaucer’s sounded final 'e') can be used to reconcile natural-sounding speech with metrical needs; awareness of pronunciation aids versification choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt notes that the final 'e' in Chaucer’s time was pronounced or dropped, allowing flexible metrical solutions; adopting the period’s pronunciation can make older diction seem natural and metrically appropriate.
